en: Initial Data, Conservation, and the Action

p.src: The laws of mechanics can be stated in two remarkably different ways. One description is local: specify the state now, use a differential equation, and advance the motion from one instant to the next. The other description treats an entire trajectory as a single object and selects the physical path by a stationary principle. Our purpose is to understand why both descriptions carry the same physics.

p.src: We shall approach the global principle slowly. First we return to initial data and the order of a differential equation. We then review energy and momentum, not because their elementary Newtonian derivations are the deepest proofs of those laws, but because they reveal structures that survive far beyond the derivations. Only after that preparation shall we pass from ordinary functions to functionals and uncover the action.

p.src: What the Order of a Law Demands

u.src: What the Order of a Law Demands
en: What the Order of a Law Demands

p.src: Begin in one dimension with a deliberately false law, $F=m\dot x=m\frac{dx}{dt}.$ It says that a force is needed merely to sustain motion: remove the force and the body stops at once. This is not Newtonian physics. Its value is precisely that it lets us see what a first-order equation would demand of its initial data.

p.src:
Suppose the force is prescribed by position, $F(x)=m\dot x.$ If the position is known at one instant, then $F(x)$ is known, and the law immediately supplies the velocity, $\dot x=\frac{F(x)}{m}.$ The same datum fixes the acceleration. Differentiating the force along the motion gives $\frac{dF}{dt}=\frac{dF}{dx}\dot x,$ and differentiating Eq.  gives $m\ddot x=\frac{dF}{dx}\dot x.$ Differentiate once more and use the product and chain rules: $\begin{aligned}
 m\dddot x
 &=\frac{d}{dt}\left(F'(x)\dot x\right) \\
 &=F''(x)\dot x^{\,2}+F'(x)\ddot x.
 \end{aligned}$ Thus position determines velocity, velocity and position determine acceleration, and the same chain continues through jerk and every higher time derivative. In this first-order world, one number $x(t_0)$ is enough to start the motion.

p.src:
Now replace the false law by Newton’s law, $F(x)=m\ddot x.$ Position still determines force and therefore acceleration, but it does not determine velocity. Two bodies can pass through the same point with different velocities and subsequently follow different motions. We must supply $x(t_0)=x_0,
 \qquad
 \dot x(t_0)=v_0.$ Once these two data are known, Newton’s equation supplies $\ddot x$, and successive differentiations supply the rest. The need for position and velocity is not an arbitrary convention: it is the signature of a second-order law.

p.src: Energy conservation is more general than the elementary argument we are about to give. It remains meaningful in electrodynamics, special and general relativity, and quantum mechanics. Here we ask the narrower question: under what conditions does ordinary Newtonian particle mechanics conserve $T+U$?

p.src: The qualification matters. A friction force appears to destroy mechanical energy if the resulting heat and the microscopic degrees of freedom of the environment are ignored. An even sharper counterexample is a tangential force that continually pushes a constrained particle around a circle. After one revolution the particle returns to the same position with a larger speed. Any single-valued potential has returned to its original value, while the kinetic energy has increased. Such a force cannot be written as the gradient of an ordinary potential.

p.src: Momentum and a Closed System

u.src: Momentum and a Closed System
en: Momentum and a Closed System

p.src:
Momentum enters by rewriting the same Newtonian equation. With constant mass, $F_i=m\frac{dv_i}{dt}
     =\frac{d}{dt}(mv_i).$ Define $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v.$ Then Newton’s law becomes $\mathbf F=\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}.$ In the absence of force, $\dot{\mathbf p}=0$, so a free particle carries a constant momentum. Intergalactic space is not perfectly empty, but it gives a good approximation to this ideal.

p.src: This discussion uses a specifically Newtonian picture of time. Clocks can be synchronized everywhere, all observers agree on one universal time, and time flows uniformly. We are also considering force laws with no prescribed external time dependence. These assumptions will not survive unchanged in relativity, so they should be stated rather than hidden.

p.src:
Now consider three interacting particles. Let $\mathbf F_{ab}$ mean the force on particle $a$ due to particle $b$. Internal forces give $\begin{aligned}
 \dot{\mathbf p}_1&=\mathbf F_{12}+\mathbf F_{13}, \\
 \dot{\mathbf p}_2&=\mathbf F_{21}+\mathbf F_{23}, \\
 \dot{\mathbf p}_3&=\mathbf F_{31}+\mathbf F_{32}.
 \end{aligned}$ Newton’s action–reaction law states $\mathbf F_{ab}=-\mathbf F_{ba}.$ The equal-and-opposite forces lie along the line joining the pair in the elementary central-force picture, although only their cancellation is needed here.

p.src:
Adding the three equations gives $\begin{aligned}
 \frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf p_1+\mathbf p_2+\mathbf p_3)
 &=(\mathbf F_{12}+\mathbf F_{21})
  +(\mathbf F_{13}+\mathbf F_{31})\notag\\
 &\quad+(\mathbf F_{23}+\mathbf F_{32})\notag\\
 &=0.\end{aligned}$ Therefore $\frac{d\mathbf P}{dt}=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbf P=\sum_a\mathbf p_a.$

p.src: Momentum conservation applies to radiation pressure, quantum systems, and relativistic physics, even though the simple pair-force proof cannot be carried unchanged into every one of those settings. There are three momentum laws, one for each spatial component, and one energy law. In special relativity these four quantities belong together as energy–momentum. This is a first hint that the conserved quantities have a deeper origin than the present calculations.

u.src: Stationarity in Ordinary Calculus
en: Stationarity in Ordinary Calculus

p.src: We now prepare for what is really the central law of the course: the principle of least action. The required mathematics begins with an ordinary function of one variable, $f(y)$. At a smooth local minimum, $\frac{df}{dy}=0.$ The derivative also vanishes at a smooth maximum. It can even vanish at a flat inflection point, such as the origin of $f(y)=y^3$. The first-derivative condition therefore identifies a stationary point; the second derivative and higher information distinguish the possibilities.

p.src:
For a function of many variables, stationarity must hold along every coordinate direction: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}=0
 \qquad\text{for every }i.$ Geometrically, at the bottom of a bowl there is no downhill first-order direction. The same equations also find maxima and saddles, so stationary remains the accurate word.

 \qquad\text{for every }i.$ Geometrically, at the bottom of a bowl there is no downhill first-order direction. The same equations also find maxima and saddles, so stationary remains the accurate word.

p.src:
As an example, take $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2+xy+3x+2y+7.$ The stationarity equations are $\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=2x+y+3=0, \\
 \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=x+2y+2=0.
 \end{aligned}$ Solving the linear system gives $x=-\frac43,
 \qquad
 y=-\frac13.$ The constant $7$ never enters the equations because a vertical shift changes the value of $f$, not the location of its stationary point.

p.src: The basic mathematical problem of mechanics is to determine the trajectory of a system from suitable data. For $10^{23}$ particles, no one attempts to write every trajectory in practice; statistical or approximate descriptions are used instead. Nevertheless, the exact classical question remains well defined.

p.src: Describe a system by generalized coordinates $q_1,q_2,\ldots,q_N.$ They may be Cartesian positions, angles, orientations, latitude and longitude, or any other independent variables that locate the system in configuration space. A single particle in three-dimensional space has three such coordinates; two particles have six; $n$ unconstrained particles have $3n$.

p.src: The motion is the whole collection $\mathbf q(t)=\bigl(q_1(t),q_2(t),\ldots,q_N(t)\bigr).$ This curve through configuration space is a generalized trajectory. To begin a Newtonian prediction, we specify both $\mathbf q(t_0)$ and $\dot{\mathbf q}(t_0)$. Newton’s equations then act locally: knowing where the system is and how it is moving tells us its acceleration, and hence how to advance to the neighboring point of the path.

Newton’s equations then act locally: knowing where the system is and how it is moving tells us its acceleration, and hence how to advance to the neighboring point of the path.

p.src:
There is another way to pose the problem. Instead of giving position and velocity at one time, hold the configurations fixed at two times, $\mathbf q(t_0)=\mathbf q_0,
 \qquad
 \mathbf q(t_1)=\mathbf q_1,$ and ask which trajectory connects them. In the elementary well-posed cases being considered, this supplies the same amount of boundary data as position and velocity at one time. More complicated systems or long time intervals can admit several classical paths, but each stationary path still satisfies the same equations of motion.

p.src: There are complementary global and local views. Globally, compare every curve between the endpoints and select a shortest one. Locally, break the curve into tiny pieces and focus on a point between two nearby pinned neighbors. Moving that point until the two small segments line up says simply: continue straight ahead. Applying the same local condition everywhere gives the straight line. The global extremization and the local differential equation encode the same geometry.

p.src: One tempting shortcut fails. Since the integrand in Eq.  is smallest when $y'=0$, why not set $y'=0$ at every point? Because a horizontal line will not generally meet the fixed endpoints. The admissible curves are constrained globally. Minimizing an integrand point by point while ignoring its boundary conditions solves a different problem.

p.src: Fermat’s Principle

u.src: Fermat’s Principle
en: Fermat’s Principle

p.src:
Optics supplies a more revealing functional. Suppose a layered isotropic medium has a light speed $c(y)$ that varies with height but not with direction at a fixed point. Fermat’s principle says that the physical ray makes the travel time stationary. Locally, $c(y)=\frac{ds}{dt},
 \qquad
 dt=\frac{ds}{c(y)}.$ Using Eq. , $dt=\frac{\sqrt{1+(y')^2}}{c(y)}\,dx,$ so the total time is the functional $\mathcal T[y]
 =\int_{x_1}^{x_2}
 \frac{\sqrt{1+\left(y'(x)\right)^2}}{c(y)}\,dx.$

p.src: If $c$ is constant, minimizing time is the same as minimizing distance, and the ray is straight. If light is faster higher in the medium, the best path can curve upward to spend more of its journey in the faster region. It cannot gain indefinitely by going straight up and then straight across: the vertical detour costs time without advancing toward the destination. The physical path is a compromise selected by the whole integral.

p.src: The Hanging Chain

u.src: The Hanging Chain
en: The Hanging Chain

p.src: A chain of fixed length suspended from two points supplies another variational problem. Gravity drives each small mass element downward, while the fixed length prevents every element from falling independently. The equilibrium curve minimizes the total gravitational potential energy subject to the length constraint.

p.src: The Action and the Lagrangian

u.src: The Action and the Lagrangian
en: The Action and the Lagrangian

p.src: We can now state the global formulation of mechanics. For every mechanical system there is a quantity called the action. Hold the endpoint configurations fixed and compare neighboring trajectories between them. The physical trajectory makes the action stationary.

p.src: The practical advantage can be dramatic. Imagine describing a rigid eraser by writing force equations for every microscopic constituent. The local equations exist in principle, but they hide the small set of collective variables we actually care about: translation and rotation. A suitable action written in those variables reaches the same physics far more directly. Likewise, in a frictionless block-on-wedge problem, conservation laws or a Lagrangian can avoid pages of constraint forces. A more general principle is often not only deeper but faster.

p.src: The minus sign is not a decorative convention. If $U$ is defined by $F=-dU/dx$, varying $T-U$ produces the correct sign in Newton’s equation. One could rename $-U$ as a new quantity and write a plus sign, but that new quantity would then be the negative of potential energy. Renaming the symbol does not change the relation.

p.src:
For generalized coordinates, write $L=L(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}),
 \qquad
 A[\mathbf q]
 =\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q})\,dt.$ The analogy with the earlier examples is exact at the structural level. The arc-length integrand depends on $y$ and $y'$; the optical integrand depends on $y$, $y'$, and $c(y)$; the mechanical integrand depends on $\mathbf q$ and $\dot{\mathbf q}$. In every case an integral assigns a number to a whole path with fixed endpoints.

p.src: For ordinary Newtonian particles, $L=T-U$. More general classical systems can have less familiar Lagrangians, especially when velocity-dependent interactions or fields are present. What survives is the architecture: construct the action, vary the path while holding its endpoints fixed, and set the first-order change to zero.

p.src: That derivation is the next task. Given a Lagrangian, we must learn how to turn stationary action into local equations of motion, and how to move back and forth between those equations and Newton’s law. The same technique will solve the optical least-time problem. Mechanics and geometrical optics have arrived at the same mathematical threshold from different directions.
